title: XOR with a hidden layer
description: Evaluate every input pair through both exact lecture architectures.
source: Lecture 2 - Logistic Regression + Neural Network.pdf, pages 56-58.

pages.title: XOR asks whether the inputs differ
pages.subtitle: Exclusive OR returns 1 for exactly one active input.
blocks: The two positive points lie at opposite corners of the unit square. No single straight line separates them from both negative corners.
Lecture 2, page 56: one threshold neuron cannot compute XOR. Hidden neurons create intermediate Boolean features that the output can combine.
Keep this inclusive equality convention for every neuron in the lesson.

pages.title: The three-neuron construction
pages.subtitle: These are exactly the two hidden gates and output gate on Lecture 2, page 57.
blocks: The hidden OR says at least one input is 1. Hidden NAND says they are not both 1. The output AND requires both statements to be true.
NAND has weights (-1, -1), threshold T = -1 and bias +1. OR has threshold 1; the output has threshold 2.
Compute hidden outputs first. Feed their 0/1 outputs, not their scores, into the final neuron.

pages.title: Three neurons: work through (0, 0), (0, 1)
pages.subtitle: First the two hidden decisions, then the output decision.

pages.title: Three neurons: work through (1, 0), (1, 1)
pages.subtitle: First the two hidden decisions, then the output decision.

pages.title: The two-neuron construction
pages.subtitle: Lecture 2, page 58 allows direct input-to-output connections.
blocks: The hidden neuron h is AND. The output receives x, y and h, with weights 1, 1 and -2. Its threshold is 1.
If both inputs are 1, the hidden neuron subtracts 2 at the output. This suppresses the 11 case that a simple OR would accept.
The direct edges bypass the hidden neuron. This is why this construction can use fewer neurons than the previous adjacent-layer construction.
Both constructions compute the same XOR truth table. Their allowed connections are different.

pages.title: Two neurons: work through (0, 0), (0, 1)
pages.subtitle: Use the newly calculated hidden output in the output score.
blocks: The raw inputs go directly to the output as well as to h. Never replace x and y by h.

pages.title: Two neurons: work through (1, 0), (1, 1)
pages.subtitle: Use the newly calculated hidden output in the output score.
blocks: The raw inputs go directly to the output as well as to h. Never replace x and y by h.

pages.title: Compare the actual connection patterns
pages.subtitle: Counts exclude input nodes. Every neuron contributes one bias parameter.
blocks: Left: 2 hidden + 1 output = 3 neurons; 4 input edges + 2 output edges = 6 weights; 6 + 3 biases = 9 parameters.
Right: 1 hidden + 1 output = 2 neurons; 2 hidden-input + 3 output-input edges = 5 weights; 5 + 2 biases = 7 parameters.
Depth is 2 in both: the longest path from input to output crosses two computational neurons. These are construction-specific counts.

pages.title: Your turn: equal inputs should return 1
pages.subtitle: XNOR is the complement of XOR. Add a NOT neuron after the XOR output q.
blocks: 1. Use the XOR outputs for 00, 01, 10 and 11. Calculate the new score -q and output r in each row.
2. How many neurons, weights and biases did this added gate introduce?
3. What is the new longest input-to-output depth?
The new gate uses weight -1 and bias 0. Count its bias as a parameter even though its chosen value is zero.

pages.title: Practice answer: one more layer
pages.subtitle: q is XOR; r is XNOR, so r must be 1 precisely when the original inputs agree.
blocks: Added: 1 neuron, 1 weight and 1 bias. Longest depth rises from 2 to 3 because every old path now ends at the extra NOT neuron.
Avoid: treating a circle threshold as a bias; forgetting direct edges in the two-neuron version; sending hidden scores instead of hidden outputs.
